column1: # How people actually type Arabic in Latin letters and digits (Arabizi), and
# what they mean by it. Nothing here is reachable from the phonetic rules,
# because the Arabic script throws away what the rules would need:
#  - short vowels, which it does not write at all, so only a dictionary knows
#    whether an "a" is a long ا or nothing ("kitab" is كتاب but "kalb" كلب), or
#    an "i" a long ي ("kbir" is كبير but "bint" بنت);
#  - the emphatic and paired letters a Latin letter cannot tell apart ("sa7" is
#    صح, "tayeb" طيب, "hatha" هذا, "habibi" حبيبي with h for ح);
#  - the ending: a final ة, ا or ى ("madrasa" is مدرسة, "marhaba" مرحبا,
#    "3ala" على), and the tanween ending written ا ("shukran" is شكرا);
#  - dialect pronunciation that the spelling does not follow: the Egyptian and
#    Levantine glottal stop for ق ("albi" is قلبي), the Gulf g for ق ("galbi",
#    "gal"), and the true hamza that the rules read as ق ("la2" is لأ, "masa2"
# Chat shorthand is here too, the kind that drops letters wholesale: "wlh" for
# والله, "slm" for سلام, "3ndi" for عندي, "ktr" for كتير.
# Dialects mix freely (Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, MSA); each line is the
# spelling those writers use, checked against the ar_full frequency list, which
# also chose the hamza seats (أنا, إذا). A value is one word, so "inshallah"
# is the run-together chat form انشالله rather than إن شاء الله, and
# "mashallah" ماشاءالله, the one value the list lacks. Lines the rules already
# get right are left out. It is a draft and wants an Arabic speaker's review.
# Format: spelling<TAB>arabic   (one mapping per line; # starts a comment)
# A spelling may repeat to offer several forms, most-preferred first.
